awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of Mobile Manipulation for Object Retrieval in Rehabilitation Hospitals
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project focuses on the development of an assistive robotic system that enables object retrieval and manipulation through voice commands. The technology addresses challenges in healthcare, assisted living, and service environments where individuals may have limited mobility or require assistance with daily tasks. The solution combines accessibility with automation to enhance operational efficiency while promoting user independence. When deployed in medical facilities, the system allows staff to focus on specialized care tasks rather than routine object retrieval. In residential settings, it gives users greater autonomy in their daily activities. The technology also has potential applications in industrial and commercial environments where human-robot collaboration can streamline workflows and reduce physical strain on workers. Beyond its immediate applications in healthcare and assistance, the system's ability to reliably grasp and manipulate objects opens possibilities in manufacturing, logistics, and service industries where object handling automation can increase productivity and workplace safety.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of the technology. This solution is based on the development of vision-guided robotic grasping systems that can pick up objects using input from a single camera. The underlying technology leverages physics simulation for data collection and learning, enabling successful transfer of grasping capabilities from simulated to real-world environments. The system demonstrates robust performance in grasping previously unseen objects, with even higher success rates achieved using simplified robotic hands. Research results show that the technology performs particularly well when handling familiar objects, making it suitable for deployment in structured environments where the set of target objects remains relatively constant. The technical approach combines computer vision, machine learning, and robotic control to create a reliable and adaptable object manipulation system.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project explored how advances in robotics and artificial intelligence—specifically mobile 
manipulation and robotic grasping—can be translated from research into practical, real-world 
applications. While recent progress has enabled robots to perform complex object-handling 
tasks in laboratory settings, a key challenge remains: identifying where these capabilities 
provide meaningful value in society and who would adopt such technologies.

The primary goal of this one-year project was to assess the "translation potential" of 
simulation-to-real (sim-to-real) robotic grasping systems. These systems are designed to train
 robots in virtual environments and then deploy them in the physical world, reducing 
development time and cost. Rather than focusing solely on technical performance, 
the project emphasized understanding real user needs, market demand, and pathways to 
technology adoption.

To achieve this, the research team conducted over 100 in-depth interviews with stakeholders 
across multiple sectors, including healthcare (rehabilitation hospitals), logistics, and 
manufacturing. These conversations provided critical insights into the practical challenges 
faced by potential users, such as workflow integration, reliability requirements, and cost 
constraints. A key finding was that, while rehabilitation settings offer compelling long-term 
opportunities, the most immediate and viable applications lie in small and medium-sized 
manufacturing enterprises (SMEs), particularly machine shops.

These businesses often face labor shortages and require flexible automation solutions that 
can be quickly adapted to different tasks. The project identified robotic machine tending, 
where robots load and unload parts from industrial equipment, as a promising "beachhead" 
application. In this context, sim-to-real grasping technology could enable faster and more 
intuitive reprogramming of robots, lowering the barrier to adoption and making automation 
accessible to a broader range of manufacturers.

From an intellectual merit perspective, the project advances understanding of how 
cutting-edge robotics technologies can move beyond the lab and into impactful use. 
It demonstrates the importance of integrating technical research with market discovery 
and user-centered design, offering a model for bridging the gap between innovation and 
implementation.

The broader impacts of the project include workforce development and community 
engagement. A postdoctoral researcher and two faculty members received training in 
customer discovery and market research methodologies, equipping them with valuable 
skills for future translational research and entrepreneurship. Additionally, the project 
fostered connections with local industry stakeholders, building relationships that can 
support ongoing collaboration and technology transfer.

Overall, this work contributes to the responsible and effective deployment of robotics 
technologies by aligning technical capabilities with real-world needs. By identifying practical 
entry points for adoption, the project helps accelerate the integration of intelligent robotic 
systems into industry, with potential benefits including increased productivity, improved 
working conditions, and enhanced economic competitiveness.
